description: Iberian kingdom (1230–1516) formed by the permanent union of Castile and León under Ferdinand III; drove the Reconquista's decisive phase, capturing Córdoba (1236), Seville (1248), and ultimately Granada (1492), before uniting with Aragon under the Catholic Monarchs to create the Spanish monarchy that funded Columbus's Atlantic voyages.

temporal.notes: Permanent union; later one half of Catholic Monarchs' personal union

lifecycle_phases.description: Ferdinand III permanently unites Castile and León (1230) and conquers Córdoba (1236), Seville (1248), and Cádiz, the heart of al-Andalus. Alfonso X 'the Wise' (1252–1284) is a great patron of learning (astronomical tables, legal codes, vernacular literature) but faces baronial revolt over his attempt to claim the Holy Roman Empire. The Black Death (1348) kills a third of Castile's population.

The civil war between Pedro I 'the Cruel' and Henry of Trastámara (1351–1369) ends with Pedro's murder; the Trastámara dynasty rules Castile. The 15th century sees continued conflict with Aragon, Portugal, and the Moorish kingdom of Granada, along with internal noble revolts. Isabella I's accession (1474) and her marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon (1469) creates the Catholic Monarchs who will unify Spain.

The joint reign of Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon completes the Reconquista with the fall of Granada (1492), expels the Jews (1492), and dispatches Columbus's voyage (1492). The Spanish Inquisition is established (1478). These years transform Castile from a medieval kingdom into the core of the first global empire.

rise_factors.description: The Reconquista gave Castilian monarchy a permanent religious legitimacy as the crusading arm of Latin Christianity; the Military Orders (Calatrava, Santiago, Alcántara) were permanent military institutions funded by Church resources, requiring no royal expenditure

Castile's vast sheep-herding economy (the Mesta) produced the finest wool in Europe; control of the Reconquista territories added the agricultural riches of Andalusia, making Castile the wealthiest Iberian kingdom

The Reconquista developed specialized frontier warfare techniques; the Military Orders (Santiago, Calatrava, Alcantara) provided permanent professional forces; combined arms tactics of cavalry and infantry worked in Iberian terrain
Systematic southward advance secured the Meseta, then Andalusia; each conquest added agricultural land, population, and tributary Muslims, converting military victories into fiscal expansion

Crusading ideology justified territorial expansion as holy war; papal support delegitimized Muslim rulers; Church wealth funded campaigns; the Reconquista attracted knights from across Europe seeking indulgences
Castile's conquest of Toledo (1085), Córdoba (1236), Seville (1248), and Murcia (1266) added vast agricultural and pastoral territories that more than doubled the kingdom's population and revenues.

decline_factors.description: The Trastámara civil war (1351–1369) devastated Castile's noble class and demonstrated the weakness of royal authority; repeated minority reigns and regencies through the 15th century produced an aristocratic factionalism that Isabella I had to overcome through force
Expulsion of Moors (1502) and Jews (1492) removed skilled artisans, merchants, financiers, and agricultural specialists; short-term religious unity was purchased at long-term economic cost
High Castilian nobility periodically resisted royal centralization; the Irmandiño revolts and later comunero rebellion demonstrated limits of royal power without institutional consent mechanisms

Massive imports of American silver from the 1540s created severe price inflation that eroded Castile's competitive manufacturing position, while debt burdens from Habsburg imperial wars consumed the bullion revenues.
